lebanon.t: The Mediterranean republic of many faiths, independent of France in 1943, prosperous, then torn by civil war and its neighbours' quarrels.
lebanon.o: France shaped [[s:greater-lebanon|Greater Lebanon]] around Mount Lebanon in 1920 within its [[s:french-mandate-for-syria-and-the-lebanon|mandate for Syria and the Lebanon]]. The unwritten National Pact of 1943 divided power among Maronite, Sunni and Shia communities, and independence was won that November when France, under popular and British pressure, released the government it had arrested.
lebanon.r: Beirut became the banking house and entrepot of the Arab east while a confessional parliament balanced eighteen recognised communities. The arrival of Palestinian refugees and later the [[e:palestine-liberation-organization|PLO]], and the grievances of a growing Shia south, strained the Pact until civil war broke out in 1975, drawing in Syria and Israel for fifteen years.
lebanon.e: The Taif Agreement of 1989 rebalanced the republic and ended the war; Syrian forces left in 2005 after Rafic Hariri's assassination, and Hezbollah fought Israel again in 2006. Financial collapse after 2019 and the Beirut port explosion of 2020 left the confessional state in its deepest crisis since the war.

lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.t: Soviet Lithuania, created by the annexation of 1940, which became the first Soviet republic to declare independence in 1990.
lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.o: Under the secret protocols of the [[e:molotov-ribbentrop-pact|Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact]], the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] occupied the [[s:republic-of-lithuania|Republic of Lithuania]] in June 1940. A rigged election produced a [[e:peoples-seimas|People's Seimas]] that requested admission to the [[e:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], and [[e:lithuania|Lithuania]] was annexed in August 1940, with [[e:vilnius|Vilnius]], regained in 1939, as its capital.
lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.r: Soviet rule brought nationalisation, collectivisation and [[e:deportation|mass deportations]] in 1941 and after the war. German occupation in 1941-1944 saw the murder of most of [[e:lithuania|Lithuania's]] [[e:jews|Jews]]. After 1944 armed partisans, the [[e:forest-brothers|Forest Brothers]], resisted until the early 1950s. [[e:antanas-snieckus|Antanas Sniečkus]] led the [[e:communist-party-of-the-soviet-union|Communist Party]] from 1940 to 1974, and the republic industrialised while Catholic dissent remained strong.
lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic.e: In 1988 the [[e:sajudis|Sąjūdis]] reform movement emerged, and in 1989 the Lithuanian [[e:communist-party-of-the-soviet-union|Communist Party]] under [[e:algirdas-brazauskas|Algirdas Brazauskas]] broke from [[e:moscow|Moscow]]. On 11 March 1990 the [[e:supreme-council-of-the-republic-of-lithuania|Supreme Council]] declared the restoration of the independent [[s:republic-of-lithuania|Republic of Lithuania]], recognised internationally in 1991.

later-guptas.t: A dynasty of Magadha and Malwa, unrelated by any proven tie to the imperial Guptas, that contested north India with the Maukharis and Harsha.
later-guptas.o: The Later [[e:gupta-empire|Guptas]] appear in the late 5th and 6th centuries as rulers in [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] and eastern [[e:malwa|Malwa]] after the decline of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]]. They are known mainly from the [[e:aphsad-inscription|Aphsad inscription]] of [[e:adityasena|Adityasena]], which lists the line from its founder Krishnagupta. Despite the name, there is no proven connection to the imperial Guptas.
later-guptas.r: For much of the 6th century the Later [[e:gupta-empire|Guptas]] fought the [[s:maukharis|Maukharis of Kannauj]]; one king, Kumaragupta, defeated the Maukhari Ishanavarman. [[e:mahasenagupta|Mahasenagupta]] campaigned as far as the [[e:brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]], while [[e:madhavagupta|Madhavagupta]] became a close ally of [[e:harsha|Harsha]] of the [[s:pushyabhuti-dynasty|Pushyabhuti dynasty]]. After Harsha's death [[e:adityasena|Adityasena]] revived the kingdom, performed a horse sacrifice and built temples.
later-guptas.e: The last known king, Jivitagupta II, was probably defeated in the early 8th century by [[e:yashovarman-of-kannauj|Yashovarman of Kannauj]], whose victory over a king of [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]] is celebrated in the [[e:prakrit|Prakrit]] poem [[e:gaudavaho|Gaudavaho]]. [[e:magadha|Magadha]] later fell to the [[s:pala-empire|Pala Empire]].

cr.a: Mahasenagupta of the Later Gupta dynasty

laietani.t: The Iberian people of the coast around Barcelona, known later for the wines of Laietania and their coins minted at Barkeno.
laietani.o: The Laietani lived on the coastal plain and hills between the [[e:llobregat|Llobregat]] and [[e:tordera-river|Tordera]] rivers, around modern [[e:barcelona|Barcelona]] and the [[e:maresme|Maresme]], from about the 5th century BCE. They formed part of the Iberian culture of the north-east and traded with [[s:emporion|Emporion]] and other Greek ports.
laietani.r: Their society was based on fortified hilltop towns such as Burriac and Puig Castellar, with grain storage silos and craft workshops. They minted coins with Iberian legends, including Laiesken and Barkeno. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their territory became famous for wine production, mentioned by Pliny and exported in [[e:amphora|amphorae]] across the western [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
laietani.e: The Laietani were subdued during [[e:cato-the-elder|Cato]]'s campaign of 195 BCE and absorbed into [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]]. Their hill towns were gradually abandoned for Roman foundations on the plain such as [[e:baetulo|Baetulo]], [[e:iluro|Iluro]] and, under Augustus, [[e:barcino|Barcino]], the origin of [[e:barcelona|Barcelona]].

lordship-of-meath.t: The great Anglo-Norman liberty of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy, centred on the castle of Trim.
lordship-of-meath.o: In 1172 [[e:henry-ii-of-england|Henry II]] granted the former [[s:kingdom-of-mide|Kingdom of Mide]] to [[e:hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath|Hugh de Lacy]] to balance [[e:richard-de-clare-2nd-earl-of-pembroke|Strongbow's]] power in [[s:kingdom-of-leinster|Leinster]]. De Lacy built motte castles across the territory and began the great stone castle at [[e:trim-county-meath|Trim]], which became the largest Norman castle in Ireland.
lordship-of-meath.r: [[s:kingdom-of-mide|Meath]] was a liberty with its own courts and officials. [[e:hugh-de-lacy-lord-of-meath|De Lacy]] settled English tenants, founded towns and abbeys and married a daughter of [[e:ruaidri-ua-conchobair|Ruaidri Ua Conchobair]], the high king. He was killed at [[e:durrow-abbey|Durrow]] in 1186. His son [[e:walter-de-lacy-lord-of-meath|Walter de Lacy]] recovered the lordship after a conflict with [[e:john-king-of-england|King John]] and held it until 1241.
lordship-of-meath.e: After Walter's death in 1241 the lordship was divided between his granddaughters, creating the liberties of [[e:trim-county-meath|Trim]] and [[s:kingdom-of-mide|Meath]]. Meath later formed the heart of the [[e:the-pale|English Pale]].

lordship-of-mann.t: The Isle of Man under English lords, above all the Stanley earls of Derby, who ruled it as 'Kings' and then 'Lords of Mann' for over three centuries.
lordship-of-mann.o: After the [[e:treaty-of-perth|Treaty of Perth]] of 1266 Man passed to [[e:scotland|Scotland]], but it changed hands repeatedly in the Anglo-Scottish wars. From 1333 [[e:edward-iii-of-england|Edward III]] granted it to [[e:william-montagu-1st-earl-of-salisbury|William Montagu]], later Earl of Salisbury, and English rule became permanent. In 1405 [[e:henry-iv-of-england|Henry IV]] granted the island to [[e:john-stanley-died-1414|Sir John Stanley]].
lordship-of-mann.r: The Stanleys styled themselves [[e:lord-of-mann|Kings of Mann]] until 1504 and then Lords of Mann. The island kept the [[e:tynwald|Tynwald]], its own laws and the [[e:manx-language|Manx language]]. [[e:james-stanley-7th-earl-of-derby|James Stanley, 7th Earl of Derby]], held it for Charles I, and his wife, [[e:charlotte-stanley-countess-of-derby|Charlotte de la Tremoille]], defended it until 1651. Smuggling flourished in the 18th century because of low duties.
lordship-of-mann.e: The lordship passed to the [[e:duke-of-atholl|Dukes of Atholl]] in 1736. To end smuggling, the British government bought the sovereign rights with the [[e:revestment-act-1765|Revestment Act]] of 1765, creating the [[e:crown-dependencies|Crown Dependency]] of the [[s:isle-of-man|Isle of Man]].

later-shu.t: The second independent kingdom of Sichuan in the tenth century, a prosperous haven of poetry, painting and learning under the Meng family.
later-shu.o: After the [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]] conquered [[s:former-shu|Former Shu]] in 925, [[e:meng-zhixiang|Meng Zhixiang]] was appointed military governor at [[e:chengdu|Chengdu]]. When the Later Tang court tried to rein him in, he resisted, absorbed neighbouring eastern [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] and in 934 proclaimed himself emperor of Shu, dying months later.
later-shu.r: His son [[e:meng-chang|Meng Chang]] reigned for over thirty years in peace. [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] prospered from [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]], salt and [[e:tea|tea]], and [[e:chengdu|Chengdu's]] court became a cultural centre: the Huajian anthology of song lyrics was compiled there in 940, the bird and flower painter [[s:state-of-huang|Huang]] Quan worked in the palace, and the Confucian classics were carved in stone.
later-shu.e: In 964 the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]] invaded, and within weeks [[e:meng-chang|Meng Chang]] surrendered in 965. He was taken to [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]], where he died soon after. Heavy [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] exactions in [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] later provoked rebellions there.

limbdi-state.t: A Jhala Rajput state in Saurashtra whose ruler hosted Swami Vivekananda in 1891, one of the middle-ranking states of the Kathiawar Agency.
limbdi-state.o: The ruling family belonged to the [[e:jhala|Jhala Rajput]] clan, which also ruled [[s:dhrangadhra-state|Dhrangadhra]] and [[s:wankaner-state|Wankaner]], and tradition dates its rule at Limbdi to around 1500. Firm records begin later.
limbdi-state.r: Limbdi was an agricultural state in the [[e:jhalawad|Jhalawad]] region, known for [[e:cotton|cotton]]. Its Thakore Sahebs were noted for promoting education, and Thakore Jaswantsinhji hosted [[e:swami-vivekananda|Swami Vivekananda]] during his travels in 1891.
limbdi-state.e: Limbdi joined the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and is now in [[e:surendranagar-district|Surendranagar district]], [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

cr.a: Dr. Andreas Birken at German Wikipedia

land-of-suhu.t: A semi-independent principality on the middle Euphrates whose governors claimed ancient descent and boasted of introducing honeybees to their land.
land-of-suhu.o: Suhu stretched along the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] between [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]] and the [[e:khabur-river|Khabur]], with its centre at [[e:anah|Anat]] (modern Ana), an island town in the river. It was a recognised province of Babylonia by the 9th century BCE, and [[e:ashurnasirpal-ii|Ashurnasirpal II]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] campaigned against it in 878 BCE when it sheltered his enemies.
land-of-suhu.r: Suhu's governors ruled as hereditary lords, nominally loyal to [[e:babylon|Babylon]] but often acting independently on the caravan route along the river. In the 8th century BCE [[e:shamash-resha-usur|Shamash-resha-usur]] and his son [[e:ninurta-kudurri-usur-of-suhu|Ninurta-kudurri-usur]] left long Akkadian inscriptions describing canal building, the defeat of Aramean raiders and, in Shamash-resha-usur's case, bringing honeybees from the mountains of the Habha people and learning to make honey and wax. Its population mixed [[e:babylonians|Babylonians]] and [[e:aramaeans|Arameans]].
land-of-suhu.e: Suhu later came under Assyrian control. The [[e:babylonian-chronicles|Babylonian Chronicle]] records that [[e:nabopolassar|Nabopolassar]] of the [[s:chaldean-empire|Chaldean Empire]] took Suhu in 616 BCE as he advanced against [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]], ending its separate identity.

larsa.t: The Amorite kingdom of the sun god's city that dominated southern Mesopotamia under Rim-Sin before falling to Hammurabi of Babylon.
larsa.o: Larsa was an old Sumerian city sacred to Utu ([[e:utu|Shamash]]), whose temple was the [[e:e-babbar|E-babbar]]. After the fall of Ur, an Amorite chief, [[e:naplanum|Naplanum]], established himself there around 2025 BCE. Larsa long stood in the shadow of [[s:isin|Isin]] until [[e:gungunum|Gungunum]], around 1932 BCE, seized Ur and its Gulf trade and claimed the old royal titles.
larsa.r: Larsa's kings ruled an irrigated plain of barley, dates and sheep, controlled canals vital to rival cities and used Sumerian for royal inscriptions and Akkadian for letters and contracts. Around 1834 BCE an Amorite leader from Emutbal with an Elamite name, [[e:kudur-mabuk|Kudur-Mabuk]], installed his sons [[e:warad-sin|Warad-Sin]] and then [[e:rim-sin-i|Rim-Sin I]] as kings. Rim-Sin's sixty-year reign was the longest in Mesopotamian history; he conquered [[s:uruk|Uruk]] and in 1794 BCE took [[s:isin|Isin]], uniting the south.
larsa.e: [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi of Babylon]] besieged Larsa and captured [[e:rim-sin-i|Rim-Sin]] in 1763 BCE, absorbing the kingdom into the [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]]. Southern resentment surfaced later in revolts under Hammurabi's son [[e:samsu-iluna|Samsu-iluna]], and the far south soon broke away under the [[s:sealand-dynasty|Sealand dynasty]].

licchavi-kingdom-of-nepal.t: The first historically documented kingdom of the Kathmandu Valley, whose Sanskrit inscriptions and temples laid the foundations of Nepalese culture.
licchavi-kingdom-of-nepal.o: The [[e:licchavi|Licchavis]] of [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] claimed descent from the ancient Licchavi clan of [[e:vaishali|Vaishali]], part of the [[s:vajji|Vajji]] league in [[e:india|India]]. They were established in the [[e:kathmandu-valley|Kathmandu Valley]] by the 5th century, succeeding the [[s:kirata-dynasty|Kirata dynasty]] of tradition. The earliest dated inscription of [[e:nepal|Nepal]], set up by King [[e:manadeva-i|Manadeva I]] at [[e:changu-narayan-temple|Changu Narayan]] in 464, records his military campaigns.
licchavi-kingdom-of-nepal.r: [[e:licchavi|Licchavi]] kings ruled through officials and village councils, and their many [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] inscriptions record land grants, water channels and temple endowments. Both [[e:shaivism|Shaiva]] [[e:hinduism|Hinduism]], centred on [[e:pashupatinath-temple|Pashupatinath]], and [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] flourished. In the early 7th century the powerful minister [[e:amshuvarman|Amshuvarman]] took royal titles and built the Kailashakuta palace. The valley grew rich as a staging post on the trade route between [[e:india|India]] and [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]].
licchavi-kingdom-of-nepal.e: Under [[e:narendradeva|Narendradeva]], restored with Tibetan help, the kingdom acknowledged Tibetan influence. Inscriptions thin out after the mid-8th century, and the valley's history becomes obscure until the [[s:thakuri-dynasty|Thakuri dynasty]] appears in 879. The [[e:nepal-sambat|Nepal Sambat]] era of 879 marks that new beginning.

cr.a: Smith, Vincent Arthur, 1848-1920Edwardes, S. M. (Stephen Meredyth), 1873-1927

lordship-of-rostock.t: Short-lived Mecklenburg lordship of the Niklotid princes around the Hanseatic port of Rostock, which fell under Danish and then Mecklenburg rule.
lordship-of-rostock.o: When [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Prince Henry]] [[e:henry-borwin-ii-lord-of-mecklenburg|Borwin II]] of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] died in 1226, his lands were divided among his sons in 1229. [[e:henry-borwin-iii-lord-of-rostock|Henry Borwin III]] received the share around Rostock, a town that had received [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] law in 1218. He and his heirs ruled as lords of Rostock, one of four Mecklenburg branches alongside Mecklenburg, [[s:lordship-of-werle|Werle]] and Parchim-Richenberg.
lordship-of-rostock.r: The lords were descendants of the Obotrite prince [[e:niklot|Niklot]], ruling a land newly settled by German farmers and townspeople. Rostock itself grew fast as a Hanseatic port and gained wide self-government, often at odds with its lords. The territory was small and the lords were pressed by [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and their [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] cousins, and in 1300 [[e:nicholas-the-child|Nicholas the Child]] placed himself under Danish protection.
lordship-of-rostock.e: After [[e:nicholas-the-child|Nicholas the Child]] died without a son in 1314, the lordship passed under Danish control and then to [[e:henry-ii-lord-of-mecklenburg|Henry II of Mecklenburg]], who secured it by 1323. Rostock remained part of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]], while the city kept its Hanseatic autonomy.

lilybaeum.t: Carthaginian fortress city at Sicily's western tip, founded after the fall of Motya, which withstood Pyrrhus and a nine-year Roman siege.
lilybaeum.o: After [[e:dionysius-i-of-syracuse|Dionysius I]] destroyed [[s:motya|Motya]] in 397 BCE, [[e:carthage|Carthage]] settled the survivors on Cape Lilybaeum, the westernmost point of [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. The new city, on a headland with a sheltered harbour facing [[e:africa|Africa]], became Carthage's main base on the island.
lilybaeum.r: Lilybaeum was a heavily fortified port with walls, towers and a deep ditch. Its population was mainly Punic with Greek elements, and its trade linked [[e:carthage|Carthage]] with [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. It successfully resisted Pyrrhus in 276 BCE and, in the First Punic War, a Roman siege by land and sea from 250 to 241 BCE.
lilybaeum.e: [[e:carthage|Carthage]] ceded Lilybaeum to [[e:rome|Rome]] by the treaty ending the [[e:first-punic-war|First Punic War]] in 241 BCE. It became the seat of one of the quaestors of Roman [[e:sicily|Sicily]], a post [[e:cicero|Cicero]] held in 75 BCE. It later became the Arab port of [[e:marsala|Marsa Allah]], modern Marsala.

lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.t: Island lordship of the Venetian Ghisi family in the Cyclades, which ended when the last Ghisi bequeathed Tinos and Mykonos to Venice in 1390.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.o: The brothers Andrea and [[e:geremia-ghisi|Geremia Ghisi]], Venetian nobles, conquered [[e:tinos|Tinos]] and [[e:mykonos|Mykonos]] around 1207 in the wave of private Venetian ventures that followed the Fourth Crusade. They also acquired other small islands, including parts of the [[e:northern-sporades|Northern Sporades]], and recognised the suzerainty of the [[s:latin-empire|Latin Empire]] and [[e:venice|Venice]].
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.r: The Ghisi held the islands as a hereditary family domain, ruling from the hilltop castle of [[e:exobourgo|Exobourgo]] on [[e:tinos|Tinos]] over Greek farmers and fishermen, and were drawn into the feudal politics of the [[s:triarchy-of-negroponte|Triarchy of Negroponte]] and the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]]. Byzantine raids under [[e:licario|Licario]] in the 1270s cost them some islands.
lordship-of-tinos-and-mykonos.e: Turkish raids grew in the 14th century. [[e:giorgio-iii-ghisi|Giorgio III Ghisi]], the last of the line, died in 1390 and left his islands to [[e:venice|Venice]], which ruled [[e:tinos|Tinos]] until 1715 as [[s:venetian-tinos|Venetian Tinos]].

latin-empire.t: Crusader state founded in Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204, a weak empire that lasted fifty-seven years.
latin-empire.o: The [[e:fourth-crusade|Fourth Crusade]], diverted by Venetian interests and Byzantine politics, stormed [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in April 1204 and plundered it. The crusaders elected Baldwin of [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]] emperor and divided the Byzantine lands: one quarter to the emperor, the rest split between [[e:venice|Venice]] and the crusader barons, who received fiefs across [[e:thrace|Thrace]], Macedonia and [[e:greece|Greece]].
latin-empire.r: The emperors ruled with Western feudal institutions, while [[e:venice|Venice]] controlled a share of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] and its trade. A [[e:latin|Latin]] patriarch replaced the [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] one, alienating the Greek population. [[e:baldwin-i-latin-emperor|Baldwin I]] was captured by the Bulgarian tsar [[e:kaloyan-of-bulgaria|Kaloyan]] at [[e:edirne|Adrianople]] in 1205. His brother [[e:henry-of-flanders|Henry of Flanders]] proved an able ruler, but after him the empire shrank to little more than the capital.
latin-empire.e: [[e:baldwin-ii-of-constantinople|Baldwin II]] pawned relics, including the [[e:crown-of-thorns|Crown of Thorns]] sold to [[e:louis-ix-of-france|Louis IX]], and even his son to raise money. In July 1261 troops of the [[s:empire-of-nicaea|Empire of Nicaea]] entered [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], Baldwin fled, and the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] was restored.

lemovices.t: Gallic people of the Limousin who sent ten thousand men to relieve Alesia and whose name survives in Limoges.
lemovices.o: The Lemovices held the granite uplands of the western [[e:massif-central|Massif Central]], in the modern [[s:viscounty-of-limoges|Limousin]]. Caesar lists them among the allies of [[e:vercingetorix|Vercingetorix]].
lemovices.r: Their land was rich in gold, which was mined in many small workings before the Roman conquest. Their main oppidum was at Villejoubert, near Saint-Denis-des-Murs.
lemovices.e: In 52 BCE they sent ten thousand men to Alesia, and their leader Sedullus was killed there. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their capital was [[e:limoges|Augustoritum]], later Lemovices, from which come Limoges and the [[s:viscounty-of-limoges|Limousin]].

las-bela-state.t: A Baloch coastal principality south of Kalat ruled by the Jams of Las Bela, which joined Pakistan in 1948.
las-bela-state.o: Around 1742 Jam Ali Khan of the Aliani branch of the Jamot tribe established a ruling house in the Las Bela plain, which lies between the [[e:kirthar-mountains|Kirthar range]] and the [[e:arabian-sea|Arabian Sea]]. The state acknowledged the overlordship of the [[s:khanate-of-kalat|Khanate of Kalat]].
las-bela-state.r: The Jam ruled a small, sparsely populated land of herders and farmers, with the port of [[e:sonmiani|Sonmiani]] as its outlet to the sea. Under British paramountcy it was handled through the [[e:baluchistan-agency|Baluchistan Agency]], and its rulers balanced between [[s:khanate-of-kalat|Kalat]] and the British. Its people spoke Lasi, [[e:balochi-language|Balochi]] and Sindhi.
las-bela-state.e: [[e:jam-ghulam-qadir-khan|Jam Ghulam Qadir Khan]] acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] in March 1948. Las Bela joined the [[s:baluchistan-states-union|Baluchistan States Union]] in 1952 and was merged into [[e:west-pakistan|West Pakistan]] in 1955; it is now a district of [[e:balochistan|Balochistan]] province.

lupaca-kingdom.t: An Aymara kingdom on the western shore of Lake Titicaca whose vast llama herds and valley colonies made it one of the richest highland realms.
lupaca-kingdom.o: After the collapse of [[s:tiwanaku|Tiwanaku]], Aymara-speaking groups formed several kingdoms around [[e:lake-titicaca|Lake Titicaca]]. The Lupaca, or Lupaqa, emerged by the 12th century on the southwestern shore of the lake in present-day [[e:peru|Peru]], with [[e:chucuito|Chucuito]] as their capital, and became rivals of the [[s:colla-kingdom|Colla Kingdom]] to the north.
lupaca-kingdom.r: The Lupaca kingdom had two paramount lords, reflecting the Andean division into upper and lower halves, and was divided into seven provinces. Its wealth lay in vast herds of llamas and alpacas. The Lupaca controlled colonies in the warm Pacific valleys of [[e:moquegua|Moquegua]] and Sama, where they grew [[e:maize|maize]] and [[e:cotton|cotton]], a pattern called the vertical archipelago. Fortified hilltop towns called pukaras reflect frequent warfare.
lupaca-kingdom.e: The Lupaca under their lord Cari defeated the [[s:colla-kingdom|Colla]] around 1450 and allied with the [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] ruler [[e:viracocha-inca|Viracocha Inca]]. They were absorbed into the [[s:inca-empire|Inca Empire]] under [[e:pachacuti|Pachacuti]]. A Spanish inspection of [[e:chucuito|Chucuito]] in 1567 by Garci [[e:diez|Diez]] de San Miguel is a major source on their society.

landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.t: A short-lived Hessian landgraviate on the middle Rhine, ruled by Philip II from Rheinfels castle above St. Goar.
landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.o: In the 1567 division of the [[s:landgraviate-of-hesse|Landgraviate of Hesse]] among the sons of [[e:philip-i-landgrave-of-hesse|Philip the Magnanimous]], the third son, [[e:philip-ii-landgrave-of-hesse-rheinfels|Philip II]], received the Lower [[s:county-of-katzenelnbogen|County of Katzenelnbogen]] on the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], with [[e:rheinfels-castle|Rheinfels]] castle above [[e:sankt-goar|St. Goar]] as his residence.
landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.r: [[e:philip-ii-landgrave-of-hesse-rheinfels|Philip II]] rebuilt [[e:rheinfels-castle|Rheinfels]] as a [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] residence and fortress, controlling the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] tolls at [[e:sankt-goar|St. Goar]] that were the territory's main income. His small state was Lutheran, like its Hessian neighbours. He married Anna [[e:elisabeth-of-the-palatinate|Elisabeth of the Palatinate]] but had no children.
landgraviate-of-hesse-rheinfels.e: When [[e:philip-ii-landgrave-of-hesse-rheinfels|Philip II]] died in 1583, his lands were divided among his brothers, most going to the [[s:landgraviate-of-hesse-kassel|Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel]], with smaller shares to Hesse-[[e:marburg|Marburg]] and [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Hesse-Darmstadt]]. [[e:rheinfels-castle|Rheinfels]] became one of the largest castles on the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] before French troops blew it up in 1797.

lordship-of-imola-and-forli.t: A short-lived papal-nephew state in Romagna, famous for the defiant Caterina Sforza, who held out against Cesare Borgia.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.o: In 1473 [[e:pope-sixtus-iv|Pope Sixtus IV]] acquired [[e:imola|Imola]] for his nephew [[e:girolamo-riario|Girolamo Riario]], who married [[e:caterina-sforza|Caterina Sforza]], daughter of [[e:galeazzo-maria-sforza|Galeazzo Maria Sforza]] of the [[s:duchy-of-milan|Duchy of Milan]]. In 1480 the pope added Forlì after the end of the [[s:lordship-of-forli|Lordship of Forli]].
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.r: [[e:girolamo-riario|Girolamo]] ruled harshly and taxed heavily, and was involved in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici in 1478. He was murdered in 1488 by the Orsi family; [[e:caterina-sforza|Caterina]] held the fortress of [[e:rocca-di-ravaldino|Ravaldino]], saved the state and governed as regent for her son [[e:ottaviano-riario|Ottaviano Riario]], crushing her enemies. She dealt with [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] and [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] as an equal and became a celebrated figure.
lordship-of-imola-and-forli.e: [[e:cesare-borgia|Cesare Borgia]] attacked in late 1499. [[e:imola|Imola]] fell quickly, and in January 1500 [[e:caterina-sforza|Caterina]] was captured at [[e:rocca-di-ravaldino|Ravaldino]] after a fierce defence. Both towns became part of Cesare's [[s:duchy-of-romagna|Duchy of Romagna]].

lato.t: Dorian hill city of eastern Crete with one of the best-preserved Greek town centres on the island, home of Alexander's admiral Nearchus.
lato.o: Lato stood in a saddle between two hills above the [[e:gulf-of-mirabello|Gulf of Mirabello]] in eastern [[e:crete|Crete]]. Founded by [[e:dorians|Dorian Greeks]], it was a city by the 7th century BCE, named after the goddess [[e:leto|Leto]].
lato.r: Lato's remains include an [[e:agora|agora]], a prytaneion, a temple and stepped theatral area, showing the civic life of a Cretan polis with [[e:kosmoi|kosmoi]] magistrates. [[e:nearchus|Nearchus]], [[e:alexander-the-great|Alexander the Great's]] admiral, came from Lato. Inscriptions record its wars and treaties with neighbours such as [[e:olous|Olous]] and [[s:hierapytna|Hierapytna]].
lato.e: Lato's harbour, Lato pros Kamara, grew in importance in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]]. After the Roman conquest of 67 BCE the hill town declined and the coastal settlement became the main centre, forerunner of modern [[e:agios-nikolaos|Agios Nikolaos]].

ligures.t: Ancient peoples of the north-western Mediterranean coast and Alps, from the Arno to the Rhône, who resisted Rome in their mountains for nearly two centuries.
ligures.o: The Ligures were among the oldest recorded peoples of north-western [[e:italy|Italy]] and southern [[e:gaul|Gaul]], already named by Greek writers of the 6th century BCE as living around [[s:massalia|Massalia]] and the Gulf of [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]]. Their origins are obscure; their language survives only in place names and personal names, and its relationship to Celtic and other [[e:indo-european-languages|Indo-European languages]] is debated.
ligures.r: They lived as separate tribes, among them the [[e:ingauni|Ingauni]], [[e:intemelii|Intimilii]], [[e:apuani|Apuani]] and [[e:statielli|Statielli]], in [[e:hill-fort|hill forts]] and upland villages, combining herding, small-scale farming and raiding. Classical authors described them as hardy and poor. They served as [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] for [[e:carthage|Carthage]], and along the coast they traded with Greek [[s:massalia|Massalia]] and the [[e:etruscans|Etruscans]], while inland groups mixed with Celtic neighbours.
ligures.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] fought the Ligures from 238 BCE onward, deporting thousands of [[e:apuani|Apuani]] to [[s:samnite-league|Samnium]] in 180 BCE. The last Alpine groups were subdued under Augustus, whose Trophy at [[e:tropaeum-alpium|La Turbie]] (7–6 BCE) lists conquered tribes. The region became Augustus's Regio IX, [[e:liguria|Liguria]], a name that survives in the modern Italian region.
