league-of-corinth.t: Alliance of Greek states under Macedonian leadership created by Philip II after Chaeronea, the framework for Alexander the Great's invasion of Persia.
league-of-corinth.o: After defeating [[s:athens|Athens]] and [[s:thebes|Thebes]] at [[e:battle-of-chaeronea-338-bce|Chaeronea]] in 338 BCE, [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II]] called the Greek states to [[s:corinth|Corinth]] in 338-337 BCE. They swore to a common peace, forbidding wars and revolutions among members, and named Philip hegemon of a war of revenge against [[e:persia|Persia]]. [[s:sparta|Sparta]] alone refused to join.
league-of-corinth.r: A council (synedrion) of delegates, with votes roughly proportional to each member's military strength, met at [[s:corinth|Corinth]] and other festival sites and could judge disputes. Members kept their own governments, but Macedonian garrisons held Corinth, [[s:thebes|Thebes]], [[s:chalcis|Chalcis]] and [[s:ambracia|Ambracia]]. Alexander had his leadership confirmed in 336 BCE and punished [[e:thebes-greece|Thebes]]' revolt in 335 BCE in the league's name.
league-of-corinth.e: The alliance gave Alexander a Greek mandate for his Asian campaign. On news of his death in 323 BCE, [[s:athens|Athens]] and the [[e:aetolians|Aetolians]] led the [[e:lamian-war|Lamian War]]; [[e:antipater|Antipater's]] victory at [[e:battle-of-crannon|Crannon]] in 322 BCE ended both the war and the league. [[e:antigonus-i-monophthalmus|Antigonus]] and Demetrius briefly revived it in 302 BCE.

lukka.t: Lukka, a land of independent communities in south-western Anatolia, known as raiders and seafarers in Hittite and Egyptian texts.
lukka.o: The Lukka lands lay in the coastal mountains of south-western [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], in later [[s:lycian-dynasts|Lycia]] and [[e:pisidia|Pisidia]]. Hittite records from the 15th century BCE show them as Luwian-speaking communities without a single king, outside or at the edge of Hittite authority.
lukka.r: Lukka people served the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] as troops, fighting at [[s:kadesh|Kadesh]], and raided neighbours by sea; an [[e:akhetaten|Amarna]] letter from the king of [[s:kingdom-of-alashiya|Alashiya]] complains of their yearly attacks. They had no central government, which made them hard to control.
lukka.e: Lukka appear among the [[e:sea-peoples|Sea Peoples]] who attacked [[e:egypt|Egypt]] under [[e:merneptah|Merneptah]] in the late 13th century BCE. After the Hittite collapse their land became the heartland of the later [[e:lycians|Lycians]], whose name continues theirs.

later-baekje.t: A rebel kingdom of southwestern Korea that revived the name of Baekje and fought Goryeo and Silla during the Later Three Kingdoms period.
later-baekje.o: [[e:gyeon-hwon|Gyeon Hwon]], a [[s:silla|Silla]] soldier, rose in revolt in 892 amid peasant uprisings against the weakened Silla court and seized much of the southwest. In 900 he proclaimed himself king at [[e:jeonju|Wansanju]], modern Jeonju, claiming to avenge the old kingdom of [[s:baekje|Baekje]] destroyed by Silla.
later-baekje.r: Later [[s:baekje|Baekje]] controlled the fertile [[e:jeolla-province|Jeolla]] region, maintained diplomatic relations with the [[s:wuyue|Wuyue]] kingdom and [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]] in [[e:china|China]], and fielded strong armies. In 927 [[e:gyeon-hwon|Gyeon Hwon]] sacked the [[s:silla|Silla]] capital at [[e:gyeongju|Gyeongju]] and forced [[e:gyeongae-of-silla|King Gyeongae]] to kill himself, then defeated [[e:taejo-of-goryeo|Wang Geon]] of [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] near [[e:daegu|Daegu]].
later-baekje.e: In 935 [[e:gyeon-hwon|Gyeon Hwon's]] son [[e:gyeon-singeom|Singeom]] deposed and imprisoned him; Gyeon Hwon escaped to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]]. In 936 [[e:taejo-of-goryeo|Wang Geon]], with Gyeon Hwon in his army, defeated Singeom at the [[e:battle-of-illicheon|Illicheon]] river, and Later [[s:baekje|Baekje]] was annexed, completing Goryeo's reunification.

lordship-of-tyre.t: The Crusader lordship of Tyre, saved by Conrad of Montferrat in 1187 and later held by the Montfort family until the end of Outremer.
lordship-of-tyre.o: [[s:tyre|Tyre]], taken by the [[e:crusader-states|Crusaders]] with Venetian help in 1124, was part of the royal domain of the [[s:kingdom-of-jerusalem|Kingdom of Jerusalem]]. In 1187, when [[e:saladin|Saladin's]] victory left almost every other town lost, [[e:conrad-of-montferrat|Conrad of Montferrat]] arrived and held [[e:tyre|Tyre]] against him, ruling it as his own base.
lordship-of-tyre.r: [[s:tyre|Tyre]] was the launching point of the [[e:third-crusade|Third Crusade]] and, with [[e:acre|Acre]], the kingdom's main port, with large Venetian and Genoese quarters. In the 1230s-1240s it was a stronghold of Frederick II's officials until the [[e:house-of-ibelin|Ibelins]] took it in 1243. From 1246 [[e:philip-of-montfort|Philip of Montfort]] held it as a lordship and built up its trade; he was killed by an [[e:order-of-assassins|Assassin]] in 1270.
lordship-of-tyre.e: His son [[e:john-of-montfort|John of Montfort]] and later heirs held it until 1291, when, after the fall of [[e:acre|Acre]], the [[e:mamluk|Mamluks]] took [[s:tyre|Tyre]] without resistance.

lordship-of-pappenheim.t: The Franconian lordship of the hereditary imperial marshals of Pappenheim, a family famous for the cavalry general of the Thirty Years' War.
lordship-of-pappenheim.o: The lords of Pappenheim, ministerials of the [[e:hohenstaufen|Staufer]], appear around 1141 in the [[e:altmuhl|Altmühl]] valley. They held the office of imperial marshal, later hereditary arch-marshal deputies to the Elector of [[e:saxony|Saxony]], which gave the small family a prominent ceremonial role at coronations and diets.
lordship-of-pappenheim.r: The lordship around the castle and town of Pappenheim was small, but the family's members served emperors widely. [[e:gottfried-heinrich-graf-zu-pappenheim|Gottfried Heinrich of Pappenheim]] was a leading imperial cavalry commander in [[e:thirty-tyrants|the Thirty]] Years' War, killed at [[e:battle-of-lutzen-1632|Lützen]] in 1632. The family became counts in 1628. The town converted to [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]].
lordship-of-pappenheim.e: Pappenheim was mediatised in 1806 and absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]], though the counts kept their castle and estates. The marshal office ended with the dissolution of the Empire in 1806.

livonian-order.t: Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, which ruled most of medieval Latvia and Estonia and fought Russia and Lithuania for three centuries.
livonian-order.o: After the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]] were destroyed at [[e:battle-of-saule|Saule]] in 1236, the survivors were incorporated into the [[e:teutonic-order|Teutonic Order]] in 1237, with [[e:hermann-balk|Hermann Balk]] as first master in [[s:livonian-confederation|Livonia]]. The Order inherited the [[e:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Sword Brothers]]' castles and lands and their role as the military power of [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]].
livonian-order.r: The Order's knights, mostly from [[e:westphalia|Westphalia]] and the [[e:rhineland|Rhineland]], governed districts from stone castles under commanders and advocates, with headquarters at Riga and later [[e:cesis|Wenden]] (Cēsis). Defeats included [[e:battle-on-the-ice|Lake Peipus]] in 1242 against [[e:alexander-nevsky|Alexander Nevsky]] and [[e:battle-of-durbe|Durbe]] in 1260, but it conquered [[e:courland|Courland]] and [[s:semigallians|Semigallia]] and bought [[s:duchy-of-estonia-1219-1346|Danish Estonia]] in 1346. It fought long wars with the archbishops of Riga and with the city itself.
livonian-order.e: Master [[e:wolter-von-plettenberg|Wolter von Plettenberg]] defeated [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Muscovy]] at [[e:battle-of-lake-smolino|Smolina]] in 1502, but the [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]] from 1558 was a disaster, with defeat at [[e:battle-of-ergeme|Ergeme]] in 1560. In 1561 the last master, [[e:gotthard-kettler|Gotthard Kettler]], secularised the Order's lands, becoming Duke of [[e:courland|Courland]] and [[s:semigallians|Semigallia]] under Polish-Lithuanian [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]].

lordship-of-bandar-rig.t: A small Arab-ruled port on the Persian coast of the Gulf, notorious under Mir Muhanna for piracy and the seizure of Kharg island from the Dutch.
lordship-of-bandar-rig.o: [[e:bandar-rig|Bandar Rig]], north of [[e:bushehr|Bushehr]], was ruled in the 18th century by the Za'ab, an Arab family settled on the Persian shore. After the death of [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] in 1747 central authority collapsed, and [[e:mir-nasir-of-bandar-rig|Mir Nasir]] governed the port as a local lord with links to the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] on nearby [[e:kharg-island|Kharg]].
lordship-of-bandar-rig.r: The lordship lived from fishing, trade and raiding. In 1753 [[e:mir-nasir-of-bandar-rig|Mir Nasir]]'s son [[e:mir-muhanna|Mir Muhanna]] killed his father and took power. He became the most feared pirate of the northern Gulf, attacking shipping and coastal towns. In 1765 he drove the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] out of their fortified trading post on [[e:kharg-island|Kharg]] and occupied the island.
lordship-of-bandar-rig.e: [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan]] of the [[s:zand-empire|Zand Empire]] sent forces against him, and in 1769 [[e:mir-muhanna|Mir Muhanna]] fled to [[e:basra|Basra]], where he was executed by the Ottoman authorities. [[e:bandar-rig|Bandar Rig]] came under [[e:zand-dynasty|Zand]] control.

leontini.t: Inland Chalcidian city of eastern Sicily on a rich grain plain, whose envoy Gorgias drew Athens into Sicilian affairs in 427 BCE.
leontini.o: [[e:thucydides|Thucydides]] records that Chalcidians from [[s:naxos|Naxos]], led by [[e:theocles|Theocles]], founded Leontini in 729 BCE, expelling the native [[e:sicels|Sicels]] from the site. It lay on hills above the Leontine plain, one of the most fertile grain-growing areas in [[e:sicily|Sicily]], a short distance inland from the sea.
leontini.r: Leontini's wealth came from grain. Around 610 BCE Panaetius became the first known tyrant in [[e:sicily|Sicily]] there. The city fell under [[e:hippocrates-of-gela|Hippocrates of Gela]] around 495 BCE and later under [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]]. Under pressure from Syracuse it sent the orator [[e:gorgias|Gorgias]] to [[s:athens|Athens]] in 427 BCE, and his speeches won an Athenian alliance and the first Athenian expedition to Sicily; Gorgias also helped bring Sicilian rhetoric to [[e:greece|Greece]].
leontini.e: In 422 BCE the Leontine aristocrats expelled the common people and moved to [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]], which absorbed the city. Its plight was a pretext for the great Athenian expedition of 415 BCE. Leontini was later revived as a dependent town and as Lentini survives today.

lohara-dynasty.t: The last major Hindu dynasty of Kashmir, under which Kalhana wrote his chronicle, the Rajatarangini.
lohara-dynasty.o: In 1003 Queen [[e:didda|Didda]] of the [[s:parvagupta-dynasty|Parvagupta dynasty]] was succeeded by her nephew [[e:sangramaraja|Sangramaraja]], a prince of Lohara, a hill state in the [[e:pir-panjal-range|Pir Panjal]] range. He founded the Lohara dynasty and resisted [[e:mahmud-of-ghazni|Mahmud of Ghazni]], whose attacks on the fortress of [[e:lohkot|Lohkot]] in 1015 and 1021 failed.
lohara-dynasty.r: The dynasty's reign was marked by struggles between kings and the landed [[e:damaras|Damaras]]. King [[e:harsha-of-kashmir|Harsha]], who ruled from 1089 to 1101, was a cultured patron but melted down temple images to pay his troops, and was killed in a revolt. A second branch began with [[e:uchchala|Uchchala]]. Under [[e:jayasimha-of-kashmir|Jayasimha]], [[e:kalhana|Kalhana]] wrote the [[e:rajatarangini|Rajatarangini]] in 1148 to 1149, a [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] verse history of [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]] and one of the few true histories of early [[e:india|India]].
lohara-dynasty.e: Later Lohara kings were weak. After a Mongol raid under [[e:zulju|Dulucha]] in 1320, the Ladakhi prince Rinchan seized power, and in 1339 [[e:shah-mir|Shah Mir]] founded the [[s:kashmir-sultanate|Sultanate of Kashmir]], ending [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] rule.

lusitanians.t: The fierce Iron Age people of central Portugal whose leader Viriathus defeated Roman armies for years before his murder in 139 BCE.
lusitanians.o: The Lusitanians lived between the [[e:douro|Douro]] and the [[e:tagus|Tagus]], in central Portugal and the neighbouring parts of [[e:extremadura|Extremadura]], emerging as a recognisable people in the second half of the first millennium BCE. They spoke Lusitanian, an [[e:indo-european-languages|Indo-European]] language known from a handful of inscriptions in [[e:latin|Latin]] letters, such as those of [[e:cabeco-das-fraguas|Cabeço das Fráguas]].
lusitanians.r: Lusitanian society was organised in clans and hillfort communities, with warrior bands under chosen leaders and a herding and farming economy in the uplands. Raiding into the richer south was a constant feature. They worshipped local gods such as [[e:bandua|Bandua]] and [[e:endovelicus|Endovelicus]], and their warriors fought in light, mobile formations that troubled Roman legions.
lusitanians.e: After raids from 155 BCE, the Roman praetor Galba massacred thousands under a false truce in 150 BCE. [[e:viriathus|Viriathus]], a survivor, led resistance until he was assassinated in 139 BCE, after which resistance collapsed. Their land later became the Roman province of [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]], a name later revived as a poetic name for Portugal.

league-of-mayapan.t: The confederation of Maya lineages that ruled northern Yucatán from the walled city of Mayapan between the fall of Chichen Itza and the 1440s.
league-of-mayapan.o: After the decline of [[s:chichen-itza|Chichen Itza]], Mayapan was founded or expanded around 1220 in western [[e:yucatan-peninsula|Yucatán]]. Colonial Maya chronicles, the books of [[e:books-of-chilam-balam|Chilam Balam]], say that the [[e:cocom|Cocom]] lineage, aided by [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] from the [[e:gulf-coast-of-mexico|Gulf Coast]], took power under the leader [[e:hunac-ceel|Hunac Ceel]], though these accounts are partly legendary.
league-of-mayapan.r: Mayapan was a densely packed walled city of about 15,000 people, with a smaller copy of [[s:chichen-itza|Chichen Itza]]'s Castillo pyramid. Leading lords of the provinces were required to live in the city, and power was shared among noble lineages headed by the [[e:cocom|Cocom]], with the [[e:tutul-xiu|Xiu]] and others. It received tribute in [[e:cotton|cotton]], honey and [[e:cacao|cacao]] and made many [[e:incense|incense]] burners for household cults.
league-of-mayapan.e: Around 1441 the [[e:tutul-xiu|Xiu]] led a revolt, the [[e:cocom|Cocom]] were massacred and the city was sacked and abandoned. Northern [[e:yucatan-peninsula|Yucatán]] split into some sixteen rival provinces, including [[s:mani|Maní]], [[s:sotuta|Sotuta]] and [[s:ah-kin-chel|Ah Kin Chel]], which the Spanish later conquered.

lordship-of-ramla.t: A lordship on the coastal plain of the Kingdom of Jerusalem that became a power base of the Ibelin family.
lordship-of-ramla.o: [[e:ramla|Ramla]], the former capital of Fatimid [[e:palestine|Palestine]], was occupied by the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] in 1099. It was under royal control at first and became a lordship around 1120, held by a family whose heiress [[e:helvis-of-ramla|Helvis]] married [[e:barisan-of-ibelin|Barisan of Ibelin]], bringing it to the [[e:house-of-ibelin|Ibelins]].
lordship-of-ramla.r: [[e:ramla|Ramla]] and the nearby castle of [[e:mirabel-castle|Mirabel]] controlled the road from [[e:jaffa|Jaffa]] to [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]] and rich farmland. The [[s:lordship-of-ibelin|Ibelin]] lords Hugh and then [[e:baldwin-of-ibelin|Baldwin of Ibelin]] held it in the later 12th century; Baldwin was among the barons who fought at [[e:battle-of-montgisard|Montgisard]] nearby in 1177. In 1186 he refused to accept [[e:guy-of-lusignan|Guy of Lusignan]] as king and left for [[s:principality-of-antioch|Antioch]].
lordship-of-ramla.e: [[e:ramla|Ramla]] fell to [[e:saladin|Saladin]] in 1187. The title was revived but the lordship was never again held by the [[s:franks|Franks]] in any lasting way.

lordship-of-biscay.t: A Basque lordship ruled by the Haro family under Navarre and Castile, whose fueros and assembly at Guernica made it a byword for local liberties.
lordship-of-biscay.o: Around 1040 [[e:inigo-lopez-ezquerra|Íñigo López Ezquerra]] appears in records as the first count or lord of [[e:biscay|Biscay]], a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]]. His descendants, the [[e:house-of-haro|López de Haro]], held the lordship for more than three centuries, moving their allegiance between Navarre and [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]].
lordship-of-biscay.r: The lords ruled with the consent of the [[e:juntas-generales-of-biscay|Juntas Generales]], the general assembly that met under the oak of [[e:guernica|Guernica]] and guarded [[e:biscay|Biscay's]] fueros, or customary laws. The economy depended on iron mining, forges, shipbuilding and fishing. In 1300 Lord [[e:diego-lopez-v-de-haro|Diego López V de Haro]] founded [[e:bilbao|Bilbao]], which grew into its chief port.
lordship-of-biscay.e: In 1379 the lordship passed by inheritance to John I of the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]], and from then on the kings of [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] ruled [[e:biscay|Biscay]] as lords. Its fueros survived until the 19th century.

locri-epizephyrii.t: Greek city in Calabria famed for the law code of Zaleucus, the earliest written Greek laws, and for its sanctuary of Persephone.
locri-epizephyrii.o: [[e:locrians|Locrians]] from central [[e:greece|Greece]] founded Locri Epizephyrii, 'Locri of the West Wind', around 680 BCE on the Ionian coast of [[e:calabria|Calabria]], near Cape Zephyrion. Ancient writers said the settlers included slaves and women of noble families, a story that may reflect the status of women in the city's aristocracy.
locri-epizephyrii.r: Locri's laws, attributed to [[e:zaleucus|Zaleucus]] in the mid-7th century BCE, were reckoned the first written code in the Greek world and known for severe punishments. A council of a thousand governed the city. Its [[e:persephone|Persephone]] sanctuary yielded hundreds of painted terracotta plaques (pinakes). Locri defeated much larger [[s:croton|Croton]] at the [[e:battle-of-the-sagra|Sagras]] river and founded [[s:hipponion|Hipponion]] and [[e:medma|Medma]]. It was Syracuse's closest ally: [[e:dionysius-i-of-syracuse|Dionysius I]] married a Locrian woman, and [[e:dionysius-ii-of-syracuse|Dionysius II]] ruled the city harshly from 356 to 346 BCE.
locri-epizephyrii.e: Locri became a Roman ally after the Pyrrhic War, went over to [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] and was retaken by [[e:scipio-africanus|Scipio]] in 205 BCE; the outrages of its commander [[e:quintus-pleminius|Pleminius]] caused a scandal in [[e:rome|Rome]]. It continued as a Roman town until abandoned in the early [[e:middle-ages|Middle Ages]].

leuci.t: Gallic people of southern Lorraine around Toul, steady suppliers of grain to Caesar's armies.
leuci.o: The Leuci lived on the upper [[e:moselle|Moselle]] and [[e:meuse|Meuse]], in the modern [[e:departement|departments]] of [[e:meurthe-et-moselle|Meurthe-et-Moselle]] and [[e:vosges|Vosges]]. Caesar mentions them among the peoples who supplied his army with grain in 58 BCE.
leuci.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their land included sanctuaries that grew important under [[e:rome|Rome]], above all Grand, a great healing shrine of [[e:apollo-grannus|Apollo Grannus]] with a large mosaic and amphitheatre.
leuci.e: The Leuci seem to have stayed loyal during the revolts, and [[e:rome|Rome]] gave them the status of a free civitas. Their chief town [[e:toul|Tullum]] became Toul, later one of the [[e:three-bishoprics|Three Bishoprics]].

later-tang.t: The second of the Five Dynasties, founded by the Shatuo Turkic ruler Li Cunxu, who claimed to restore the Tang and briefly reunited much of northern China.
later-tang.o: [[e:li-cunxu|Li Cunxu]], ruler of [[s:jin-five-dynasties|Jin (Five Dynasties)]] at [[e:taiyuan|Taiyuan]], proclaimed himself emperor of a restored Tang in 923 and within months captured [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]], ending the [[s:later-liang|Later Liang]]. He moved the capital to [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]], the old Tang eastern capital, and in 925 conquered [[s:former-shu|Former Shu]] in [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]].
later-tang.r: The ruling house and much of its army were [[e:shatuo|Shatuo Turks]]. [[e:li-cunxu|Li Cunxu]], a brilliant general, alienated his troops by favouring actors and was killed in a mutiny in 926. His adopted brother [[e:emperor-mingzong-of-later-tang|Li Siyuan (Emperor Mingzong)]] restored order, and under his minister [[e:feng-dao|Feng Dao]] work began in 932 on the first printed edition of the Confucian classics.
later-tang.e: After [[e:emperor-mingzong-of-later-tang|Mingzong]]'s death, [[e:li-congke|Li Congke]] seized the throne in 934. The governor [[e:shi-jingtang|Shi Jingtang]] rebelled at [[e:taiyuan|Taiyuan]] with Khitan help, promising them the [[e:sixteen-prefectures|Sixteen Prefectures]]. Li Congke burned himself to death in [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] as their armies arrived, and Shi Jingtang founded the [[s:later-jin-936-947|Later Jin]] (936-947).

lan-xang.t: The 'Kingdom of a Million Elephants', founded by Fa Ngum in 1353, which united the Lao lands and is the historic forerunner of modern Laos.
lan-xang.o: [[e:fa-ngum|Fa Ngum]], a Lao prince raised in exile at the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] court in [[e:angkor|Angkor]], led an army up the [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]], captured [[s:muang-sua|Muang Sua]] in 1353 and was crowned king of Lan Xang. He extended his rule over the [[e:khorat-plateau|Khorat plateau]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Vientiane]] plain, and is traditionally credited with introducing [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada Buddhism]] and the [[e:phra-bang|Phra Bang]] image from [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970|Cambodia]].
lan-xang.r: Lan Xang was a mandala of muang paying tribute to the king, with a strong Buddhist sangha. [[e:setthathirath|Setthathirath]] moved the capital from [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Luang Prabang]] to [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Vientiane]] in 1560, built the [[e:pha-that-luang|That Luang]] stupa and [[e:wat-xieng-thong|Wat Xieng Thong]], and resisted Burmese invasions. [[e:sourigna-vongsa|Sourigna Vongsa's]] long reign in the 17th century was a golden age, recorded by the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] trader [[e:gerrit-van-wuysthoff|Gerrit van Wuysthoff]].
lan-xang.e: After [[e:sourigna-vongsa|Sourigna Vongsa]] died without an undisputed heir, succession wars split the kingdom in 1707 into the [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Kingdom of Luang Phrabang]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Kingdom of Vientiane]], followed by the [[s:kingdom-of-champasak|Kingdom of Champasak]] in 1713. Lan Xang remains the foundation of Lao national identity.

lombard-league.t: An alliance of northern Italian city-republics that defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176 and won self-government from the emperors.
lombard-league.o: In 1167, according to tradition in an oath sworn at [[e:oath-of-pontida|Pontida]], [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]], [[s:commune-of-cremona|Cremona]], [[s:commune-of-bergamo|Bergamo]], [[s:commune-of-brescia|Brescia]], [[s:duchy-of-mantua|Mantua]] and other cities formed a league against [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]], absorbing the [[s:veronese-league|Veronese League]]. [[e:pope-alexander-iii|Pope Alexander III]] supported it, and the new city of [[s:commune-of-alessandria|Alessandria]] was named after him.
lombard-league.r: The league was an alliance of communes with a council of rectors from member cities, a shared war chest and joint armies, rather than a single state. Its forces defeated [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Barbarossa]] at [[e:battle-of-legnano|Legnano]] in 1176, forcing the Truce of [[e:venice|Venice]] in 1177 and the [[e:peace-of-constance|Peace of Constance]] in 1183, which recognised the cities' rights to elect their own officials.
lombard-league.e: The league was revived in 1226 against Frederick II, who defeated it at [[e:battle-of-cortenuova|Cortenuova]] in 1237 but failed to break the cities. After Frederick's death in 1250 it faded away, as the communes turned to wars among themselves and to rule by lords.

lordship-of-ibelin.t: A small Crusader lordship whose castle gave its name to the Ibelins, the most powerful noble family of Outremer and Cyprus.
lordship-of-ibelin.o: In 1141 [[e:fulk-king-of-jerusalem|King Fulk]] built a castle at [[e:yavne|Yibna]] (Yavne), on the coastal plain south of [[e:jaffa|Jaffa]], as one of a ring of forts to contain the Fatimid garrison of [[e:ashkelon|Ascalon]]. He granted it to [[e:barisan-of-ibelin|Barisan]], constable of Jaffa, whose descendants took the name of Ibelin.
lordship-of-ibelin.r: The lordship itself was small, but the family rose quickly through marriage, gaining [[e:ramla|Ramla]], [[e:mirabel-castle|Mirabel]] and [[e:nablus|Nablus]]. [[e:barisan-of-ibelin|Barisan]]'s sons Hugh, Baldwin and [[e:balian-of-ibelin|Balian of Ibelin]] were leading barons; Balian married the dowager queen [[e:maria-komnene-queen-of-jerusalem|Maria Komnene]]. The castle lost its military purpose after [[e:ashkelon|Ascalon]] fell in 1153.
lordship-of-ibelin.e: Ibelin was lost to [[e:saladin|Saladin]] in 1187, the year Balian negotiated the surrender of [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]]. The family survived the catastrophe and in the 13th century dominated [[s:beirut|Beirut]], [[e:jaffa|Jaffa]], [[e:arsuf|Arsuf]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-cyprus|Kingdom of Cyprus]].

lahsa-eyalet.t: The Ottoman province of eastern Arabia, based at Hofuf, which guarded the Gulf flank of the empire for a century.
lahsa-eyalet.o: After the conquest of [[e:iraq|Iraq]], the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] extended its reach down the [[e:persian-gulf|Gulf]] coast and took [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Hasa]] around 1550, partly to counter the Portuguese. The province of Lahsa was organised around 1560 with its seat at [[e:hofuf|Hofuf]] and included the port of [[e:qatif|Qatif]].
lahsa-eyalet.r: Governors held the oasis towns with small garrisons of [[e:janissaries|Janissaries]] and local levies, collecting taxes from the large date-growing oasis of [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Hasa]] and customs at [[e:qatif|Qatif]]. The province served as a base against [[s:portuguese-bahrain|Portuguese Bahrain]], though an Ottoman expedition to take the island in 1559 failed. Control of the [[e:bedouin|Bedouin]] hinterland was always weak, and governors were often isolated from [[e:basra|Basra]] and [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]].
lahsa-eyalet.e: In 1670 the [[e:bedouin|Bedouin]] chief [[e:barrak-ibn-ghurayr|Barrak ibn Ghurayr]] of the [[s:banu-khalid-emirate|Banu Khalid]] expelled the Ottoman garrison and founded the Banu Khalid [[e:emirate|Emirate]]. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] returned to [[e:al-ahsa-oasis|al-Hasa]] only in 1871.

lordship-of-verona.t: The Scaliger lordship that made Verona a power in north-eastern Italy, whose lord Cangrande della Scala sheltered Dante.
lordship-of-verona.o: After [[e:ezzelino-iii-da-romano|Ezzelino III da Romano]] died in 1259, the [[s:commune-of-verona|Commune of Verona]] chose [[e:mastino-i-della-scala|Mastino I della Scala]] as its leader, and by 1262 he was effectively lord. His family, the della Scala or [[e:scaliger|Scaligeri]], made the office hereditary.
lordship-of-verona.r: The [[e:scaliger|Scaligeri]] ruled [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]] as lords and imperial vicars. [[e:cangrande-i-della-scala|Cangrande I]], lord from 1311 to 1329, conquered [[s:commune-of-vicenza|Vicenza]], [[s:commune-of-padua|Padua]] and [[s:commune-of-treviso|Treviso]] and hosted the exiled [[e:dante-alighieri|Dante]], who dedicated the [[e:paradiso-dante|Paradiso]] to him. Under [[e:mastino-ii-della-scala|Mastino II]] the lordship reached [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] and [[s:commune-of-parma|Parma]], but a coalition of [[e:venice|Venice]] and [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] stripped most of it away in 1339. The family's Gothic tombs, the [[e:scaliger-tombs|Arche Scaligere]], and the [[e:castelvecchio-verona|Castelvecchio]] bridge survive.
lordship-of-verona.e: Family murders weakened the dynasty. In 1387 [[e:gian-galeazzo-visconti|Gian Galeazzo Visconti]] seized [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]] from Antonio della Scala and annexed it to the [[s:lordship-of-milan|Lordship of Milan]]. [[e:venice|Venice]] took the city in 1405.

lakhtar-state.t: A Jhala Rajput state of the Jhalawad district of northern Kathiawar, one of several branches of the Jhala clan.
lakhtar-state.o: Lakhtar was founded in 1604 by a cadet of the [[e:jhala|Jhala]] house of [[e:halvad|Halvad]], the line that also ruled [[s:dhrangadhra-state|Dhrangadhra State]]. Its seat was the small fortified town of Lakhtar, earlier known as Thana Lakhtar.
lakhtar-state.r: The Thakor ruled a dry territory of [[e:cotton|cotton]] and grain villages, paying tribute to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads of Baroda]] and, after 1807, coming under British supervision in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]]. It was a nine-gun salute state. Few further details of its rulers are widely recorded.
lakhtar-state.e: Lakhtar merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in present [[e:surendranagar-district|Surendranagar district]].

lesser-nogai-horde.t: The western branch of the Nogai Horde, which moved to the Kuban steppe and became a client of the Crimean Khanate and the Ottomans.
lesser-nogai-horde.o: In 1557, amid a civil war within the [[s:nogai-horde|Nogai Horde]] over relations with [[e:russia|Russia]], the mirza Kazy broke away with his followers and moved west across the [[e:volga|Volga]] to the steppes of the [[e:north-caucasus|North Caucasus]] and the Kuban. The new group became known as Kazy's Ulus or the Lesser Nogai Horde.
lesser-nogai-horde.r: The Lesser [[e:nogais|Nogais]] were pastoral nomads who raided Muscovite and Caucasian lands, often in alliance with the [[s:crimean-khanate|Crimean Khanate]]. They were ruled by mirzas of Kazy's line and recognised Crimean and, through it, Ottoman overlordship. Their horses and captives were traded through the Crimean ports.
lesser-nogai-horde.e: In the early 17th century many Lesser [[e:nogais|Nogais]] moved closer to the [[s:crimean-khanate|Crimean Khanate]], especially after [[s:kalmyk-khanate|Kalmyk Khanate]] pressure in the 1630s. They were absorbed into the Crimean and Kuban Nogai communities, which were later annexed by [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1783.

lordship-of-caesarea.t: A Crusader lordship on the coast of Palestine whose 13th-century walls still stand at Caesarea.
lordship-of-caesarea.o: Baldwin I took Caesarea in May 1101 with a Genoese fleet, which received a share of the spoils including a green glass bowl believed to be the [[e:holy-grail|Holy Grail]], now the [[e:sacro-catino|Sacro Catino]] in [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]]. The city became the seat of a lordship, held from about 1110 by [[e:eustace-grenier|Eustace Grenier]] and his descendants.
lordship-of-caesarea.r: Caesarea was one of the major lordships of the [[s:kingdom-of-jerusalem|Kingdom of Jerusalem]] and the seat of a [[e:latin|Latin]] archbishop. Its lords, the Grenier family and later the Aleman line, lived from the harbour and the coastal plain. The town was smaller than the Roman city, but its defences were rebuilt several times, most thoroughly by [[e:louis-ix-of-france|Louis IX]] in 1251-1252 with a sloping glacis and moat.
lordship-of-caesarea.e: [[e:saladin|Saladin]] took Caesarea in 1187; it was regained in 1191. In 1265 [[e:baybars|Baybars]] captured it after a short siege and razed its walls; [[e:john-aleman|John Aleman]] was its last lord.

lixus.t: An ancient Phoenician and Punic port on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, linked in Greek myth to the Garden of the Hesperides.
lixus.o: Lixus lay on a hill above the [[e:loukkos|Loukkos]] river near modern [[e:larache|Larache]]. [[e:pliny-the-elder|Pliny the Elder]] believed it was among the oldest Phoenician foundations, with a temple of [[e:melqart|Melqart]] older than that of [[s:gadir|Gades]]. Archaeology shows Phoenician settlers there from about the 8th century BCE, trading with the [[e:berbers|Berber]] peoples of the interior.
lixus.r: Lixus was a self-governing town with Phoenician gods and Punic language, part of the trading world of the [[s:punic-empire|Punic Empire]]. Its economy rested on fishing, fish-salting and garum production, and it traded [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], gold and grain along the Atlantic coast. Greek writers placed the [[e:garden-of-the-hesperides|Garden of the Hesperides]] and the struggle of [[e:heracles|Heracles]] with [[e:antaeus|Antaeus]] nearby.
lixus.e: After the fall of [[e:carthage|Carthage]] Lixus came under the [[s:kingdom-of-mauretania|Kingdom of Mauretania]], minting coins with Punic legends, and was fully absorbed under [[e:juba-ii|Juba II]] around 25 BCE. [[e:claudius|Claudius]] later made it a Roman colony, and its ruins, with large fish-salting works, are an archaeological site.

later-zhao.t: The kingdom of Shi Le, a former slave of Jie origin who conquered most of northern China, and of his notoriously cruel successor Shi Hu.
later-zhao.o: [[e:shi-le|Shi Le]], a [[e:jie-people|Jie]] tribesman once sold into [[e:slavery|slavery]], became the most successful general of [[s:han-zhao|Han Zhao]]. In 319 he broke away and proclaimed himself King of Zhao at [[e:xingtai|Xiangguo]] (Xingtai, [[e:hebei|Hebei]]). He captured the [[e:han-zhao|Han Zhao]] ruler [[e:liu-yao|Liu Yao]] in 328, destroyed his state in 329 and declared himself emperor in 330.
later-zhao.r: [[e:shi-le|Shi Le]], though illiterate, had the histories read to him, set up schools and recruited Chinese officials while keeping the [[e:jie-people|Jie]] and other tribal peoples as a privileged military [[e:caste|caste]]. The Buddhist monk [[e:fotudeng|Fotudeng]] advised both him and his successor, helping [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] spread in the north. [[e:shi-hu|Shi Hu]], who seized power in 334 and moved the capital to Ye, built lavish palaces and imposed crushing labour and military levies.
later-zhao.e: After [[e:shi-hu|Shi Hu's]] death in 349 his sons fought for the throne. His adopted grandson [[e:ran-min|Ran Min]] seized Ye in 350 and ordered the massacre of the [[e:jie-people|Jie]], founding [[s:ran-wei|Ran Wei]]; the last Later Zhao ruler was killed in 351.

land-chenla.t: The northern, inland half of the Khmer kingdom of Chenla after its split in the early 8th century, known only from Chinese records.
land-chenla.o: Chinese sources report that around 707 [[s:chenla|Chenla]] divided into two parts: a northern Land Chenla, Lu Zhenla, also called Wendan, which lay in the uplands of the middle [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]] in what is now southern [[e:laos|Laos]] and north-east [[s:thailand|Thailand]], and a southern [[s:water-chenla|Water Chenla]] nearer the delta.
land-chenla.r: Land [[s:chenla|Chenla]] appears more stable and unified than its southern counterpart. It sent embassies to the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] court in the 8th century, including one led by a royal heir in 753 who joined Tang forces against [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]]. Its people were Khmer-speaking, and Shaivite temples and [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] inscriptions of the period are found in the [[e:wat-phu|Wat Phu]] and Mun river region.
land-chenla.e: Land Chenla's fate after the late 8th century is unclear. Its territories were absorbed into the [[s:khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]] after [[e:jayavarman-ii|Jayavarman II]] proclaimed his rule in 802, and many historians doubt that the Chinese division matched clear political boundaries.

lamidate-of-ngaoundere.t: A Fulbe lamidate on the Adamaoua plateau of Cameroon, a sub-emirate of Adamawa and one of the great slave-raiding states of the 19th century.
lamidate-of-ngaoundere.o: Ngaoundere was founded around 1835 by [[e:ardo-njobdi|Ardo Njobdi]], a [[e:fula|Fulbe]] leader acting under the authority of the [[s:adamawa-emirate|Adamawa Emirate]]. His forces conquered the [[e:mbum-people|Mbum people]] of the [[e:adamawa-plateau|Adamaoua]] plateau and took over the site of Ngaoundere, which became the seat of a lamido owing allegiance to [[e:yola|Yola]] and, through it, to the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]].
lamidate-of-ngaoundere.r: The lamidate's [[e:fula|Fulbe]] rulers governed a large [[e:mbum-people|Mbum]] and [[e:gbaya-people|Gbaya]] population, partly incorporated as subjects and partly enslaved. Ngaoundere sent raiding expeditions far to the east and south, into what is now the [[e:central-african-republic|Central African Republic]] and [[e:chad|Chad]], and was one of the main sources of slaves in the region. [[e:cattle|Cattle]] herding on the plateau grasslands was the other pillar of its economy.
lamidate-of-ngaoundere.e: German forces reached Ngaoundere in 1901 and defeated the lamido's army, and it became part of [[s:kamerun|Kamerun]], later [[s:french-cameroon|French Cameroon]]. The Lamido of Ngaoundere still reigns from his palace in the city.

lordship-of-overijssel.t: The eastern Hanseatic lands of the former bishopric of Utrecht, with Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle, under Habsburg rule before joining the Dutch Republic.
lordship-of-overijssel.o: The Oversticht, the eastern part of the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-utrecht|Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht]], was ruled by the [[e:bishop|bishops]] until 1528, when [[e:henry-of-the-palatinate|Bishop Henry of Bavaria]] handed his temporal power to [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]]. Overijssel then became one of the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Seventeen Provinces]] of the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburg]] [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], with [[e:drenthe|Drenthe]] attached to it.
lordship-of-overijssel.r: The province was governed by estates of nobles and the three towns of [[e:deventer|Deventer]], [[e:kampen|Kampen]] and [[e:zwolle|Zwolle]], Hanseatic ports on the [[e:ijssel|IJssel]]. Deventer was the birthplace of the [[e:devotio-moderna|Devotio Moderna]] movement and a centre of [[e:printing-press|printing]]. The [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] ruled through stadtholders but left the towns their privileges.
lordship-of-overijssel.e: Overijssel joined the [[e:union-of-utrecht|Union of Utrecht]] in 1579 and, after the [[e:act-of-abjuration|Act of Abjuration]] of 1581, the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]], although Spanish troops held parts of it until the 1590s.

lordship-of-leo-sgouros.t: Short-lived domain of the Greek magnate Leo Sgouros in the north-eastern Peloponnese, the chief resistance to the Frankish conquest of southern Greece.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.o: [[e:leo-sgouros|Leo Sgouros]] inherited power as archon of [[e:nafplio|Nauplia]] from his father around 1198, as Byzantine authority weakened. He seized [[s:argos|Argos]] and [[s:corinth|Corinth]], attacked [[s:athens|Athens]] and [[s:thebes|Thebes]], and married [[e:eudokia-angelina|Eudokia]], daughter of the deposed emperor [[e:alexios-iii-angelos|Alexios III]], gaining a measure of legitimacy as [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] fell to the [[e:fourth-crusade|Fourth Crusade]] in 1204.
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.r: [[e:leo-sgouros|Sgouros]] ruled as an independent strongman from fortresses rather than through any formal state, using force and reputed cruelty, and dominating the [[e:argolid|Argolid]], the [[e:corinthia|Corinthia]] and the Isthmus. He tried to block [[e:boniface-i-marquis-of-montferrat|Boniface of Montferrat]] at Thermopylae in 1204 but retreated to the near-impregnable citadel of [[e:acrocorinth|Acrocorinth]].
lordship-of-leo-sgouros.e: Besieged by the [[s:franks|Franks]], [[e:leo-sgouros|Sgouros]] died around 1208, reportedly riding his horse off the cliffs of [[e:acrocorinth|Acrocorinth]]. Its garrison held out until about 1210, and [[s:lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia|Argos and Nauplia]] until 1212, when they fell to the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] and became the [[e:lordship-of-argos-and-nauplia|Lordship of Argos and Nauplia]].

lower-canada.t: The French-speaking British colony on the lower St Lawrence whose clashes between its elected assembly and appointed rulers led to the rebellions of 1837 and 1838.
lower-canada.o: The [[e:constitutional-act-1791|Constitutional Act]] of 1791 divided the [[s:province-of-quebec|Province of Quebec]] in two. The eastern part, along the lower [[e:st-lawrence-river|St Lawrence]] with [[e:quebec|Quebec City]] as capital, became Lower [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]], where the great majority of people were French-speaking Catholics living under French [[e:civil-law|civil law]] and the seigneurial system.
lower-canada.r: Lower [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]] had an elected assembly, but real power lay with the governor and appointed councils dominated by an English-speaking merchant elite, the so-called [[e:chateau-clique|Château Clique]]. The Parti canadien, later the Parti patriote under [[e:louis-joseph-papineau|Louis-Joseph Papineau]], controlled the assembly and demanded control of revenues. [[e:montreal|Montreal's]] merchants dominated the [[e:timber|timber]] and wheat trades, while the Catholic Church held great influence over rural life.
lower-canada.e: [[e:britain|Britain's]] refusal of reform led to armed rebellion in 1837 and 1838, crushed by troops. [[e:john-lambton-1st-earl-of-durham|Lord Durham's]] report recommended union with [[s:upper-canada|Upper Canada]] to assimilate [[e:french-canadians|French Canadians]], and the [[e:act-of-union-1840|Act of Union]] created the [[s:province-of-canada|Province of Canada]] in 1841.

luluid-aleppo.t: A brief regime in Aleppo founded by the Hamdanid chamberlain Lu'lu', who displaced his masters and ruled with Fatimid recognition.
luluid-aleppo.o: [[e:lulu-al-kabir|Lu'lu' al-Kabir]] was a slave commander and chamberlain of the [[s:hamdanid-emirate-of-aleppo|Hamdanids of Aleppo]] who had long been the real power behind the young [[e:emir|emirs]]. In 1004 he deposed the last [[e:hamdanid-dynasty|Hamdanid]] heirs and took power in his own name, recognising the Fatimid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] in [[e:cairo|Cairo]] while keeping the Byzantine tribute arrangement.
luluid-aleppo.r: [[e:lulu-al-kabir|Lu'lu']] and his son Mansur, who succeeded him around 1008, governed a small [[e:emirate|emirate]] squeezed between [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]] and threatened by the [[e:banu-kilab|Bedouin Banu Kilab]]. Mansur tried to break the Kilab by treachery, imprisoning their leaders, among them [[e:salih-ibn-mirdas|Salih ibn Mirdas]], who escaped.
luluid-aleppo.e: In 1016 the commander of the citadel, Fath al-Qal'i, handed [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] to the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]], and Mansur fled to Byzantine territory. After a period of Fatimid governors, [[e:salih-ibn-mirdas|Salih ibn Mirdas]] took Aleppo in 1024 and founded the [[s:mirdasid-emirate|Mirdasid Emirate]].

lathi-state.t: A small Gohil Rajput state in Saurashtra, best remembered for its Thakore Sursinhji, the Gujarati poet known as Kalapi.
lathi-state.o: Lathi was ruled by a branch of the [[e:gohil|Gohil Rajputs]], the clan of [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar]] and [[s:palitana-state|Palitana]]; tradition dates its founding to the 14th century. Little is recorded of its early history.
lathi-state.r: Lathi was a minor state of a few villages in the [[e:kathiawar-agency|Kathiawar Agency]]. Its ruler [[e:kalapi|Sursinhji Gohil]] (1874–1900) wrote romantic Gujarati poetry under the name Kalapi, and his collection [[e:kalapino-kekarav|Kalapino Kekarav]] made him one of the leading poets of modern Gujarati literature.
lathi-state.e: Lathi joined the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and is now a town in Amreli district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

cr.a: Unknown, person in image himself died in 1900

lordship-of-lesbos.t: Genoese lordship of the Gattilusi family on Lesbos, a Byzantine-allied dynasty that ruled northern Aegean islands until the Ottoman conquest in 1462.
lordship-of-lesbos.o: The Genoese adventurer [[e:francesco-i-gattilusio|Francesco Gattilusio]] helped the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos regain his throne in 1354. In reward John gave him his sister Maria in marriage and the island of [[e:lesbos|Lesbos]] as a dowry in 1355, making the Gattilusi hereditary lords of the island, with [[s:mytilene|Mytilene]] as their capital.
lordship-of-lesbos.r: The Gattilusi acted as Byzantine [[e:vassal|vassals]] and relatives, adopting Greek ways and titles, while trading with [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]]. Their family extended its power to [[s:aenus|Ainos]], [[s:thasos|Thasos]], [[e:lemnos|Lemnos]] and [[e:samothrace|Samothrace]]. They profited from alum, grain and the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] trade, and from the 1390s paid tribute to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. Mytilene's castle was rebuilt in their time.
lordship-of-lesbos.e: After the fall of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in 1453 the Gattilusi remained as Ottoman tributaries. In 1462 [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] besieged and took [[s:mytilene|Mytilene]]; the last lord, [[e:niccolo-gattilusio-lord-of-lesbos|Niccolo Gattilusio]], was taken to Constantinople and later executed.

lordship-of-milan.t: The signoria through which the Visconti turned Milan into the strongest state in northern Italy, before buying a ducal title in 1395.
lordship-of-milan.o: In 1259 [[e:martino-della-torre|Martino della Torre]] was made lord of the people, turning the [[s:commune-of-milan|Commune of Milan]] into a lordship. The della Torre were challenged by Archbishop [[e:ottone-visconti|Ottone Visconti]], who defeated them at [[e:battle-of-desio|Desio]] in 1277; his great-nephew [[e:matteo-i-visconti|Matteo I Visconti]] received the title of imperial vicar in 1294.
lordship-of-milan.r: The Visconti ruled through councils and appointed podestà while keeping communal forms. [[e:azzone-visconti|Azzone Visconti]] absorbed [[s:commune-of-bergamo|Bergamo]], [[s:commune-of-cremona|Cremona]], Como, [[e:lodi-dynasty|Lodi]], [[s:commune-of-brescia|Brescia]] and other cities in the 1330s. Archbishop Giovanni Visconti added [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]] and [[s:republic-of-bologna|Bologna]], and in 1359 [[e:galeazzo-ii-visconti|Galeazzo II]] took [[s:commune-of-pavia|Pavia]]. [[e:gian-galeazzo-visconti|Gian Galeazzo Visconti]] overthrew his uncle [[e:bernabo-visconti|Bernabò]] in 1385 and created a centralised state, beginning [[e:milan-cathedral|Milan Cathedral]] in 1386.
lordship-of-milan.e: In 1395 [[e:gian-galeazzo-visconti|Gian Galeazzo]] bought the title of duke from [[e:wenceslaus-iv-of-bohemia|Emperor Wenceslas]], turning the lordship into the [[s:duchy-of-milan|Duchy of Milan]], which he expanded towards [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]] and [[e:umbria|Umbria]] before his death in 1402.

lawa-state.t: A tiny Naruka Rajput chiefship in eastern Rajasthan, among the smallest polities recognised by the British in Rajputana.
lawa-state.o: Lawa was held by a branch of the Naruka [[e:kachhwaha|Kachhwaha Rajputs]], kinsmen of the rulers of [[s:alwar-state|Alwar State]], and became a separate chiefship around 1772. It later fell under [[s:tonk-state|Tonk State]], but after men acting for the Nawab of Tonk killed members of the Thakur's family in the 1860s, the British made Lawa a separate chiefship.
lawa-state.r: Lawa consisted of only a few villages and was overseen by the [[e:jaipur|Jaipur]] Residency. Its chief held the title of Thakur. Little else is recorded.
lawa-state.e: After independence Lawa was merged into the [[e:rajasthan|Rajasthan]] union in 1948; its village lies in Tonk district.

lamu.t: A Swahili island town on the Kenyan coast whose well-preserved old town is the finest surviving example of Swahili urban architecture.
lamu.o: Settlement in the Lamu archipelago goes back to at least the 9th century, and the present town grew in the 14th century as one of the Muslim trading towns of the Lamu archipelago. It was governed by a council of leading families rather than a strong dynasty, and for long competed with its larger neighbour, the [[s:pate-sultanate|Pate Sultanate]].
lamu.r: Lamu's merchants exported mangrove poles, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and grain and imported cloth and [[e:porcelain|porcelain]] from [[e:arabia|Arabia]] and [[e:india|India]]. Its elite built coral-stone houses with carved doors and plaster niches, and mosques with [[e:swahili|Swahili]] features. It paid tribute to the Portuguese in the 16th and 17th centuries and later to Pate, while its poets wrote in the Kiamu dialect of Swahili.
lamu.e: In 1812 or 1813 Lamu defeated Pate and its Mazrui allies at the [[e:battle-of-shela|Battle of Shela]], then placed itself under the protection of the [[s:omani-empire|Omani Empire]], later the [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Sultanate of Zanzibar]]. It passed to British [[s:kenya|Kenya]] with the coastal strip. [[e:lamu-old-town|Lamu Old Town]] is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

lordship-of-faenza.t: The Manfredi lordship of Faenza in Romagna, the town whose glazed pottery gave Europe the word 'faience'.
lordship-of-faenza.o: The Manfredi family led Faenza's [[e:house-of-welf|Guelphs]] in the 13th century, and in 1313 [[e:francesco-manfredi|Francesco Manfredi]] became lord of the city. The family ruled as papal vicars, though they lost and regained the city several times in the 14th century.
lordship-of-faenza.r: The Manfredi governed Faenza and neighbouring towns such as [[e:imola|Imola]] for a time, often serving as condottieri for [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]], [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] or [[e:venice|Venice]]. The town's maiolica workshops flourished in the 15th century, and their glazed earthenware gave French and English the name faience. [[e:carlo-ii-manfredi|Carlo II Manfredi]] rebuilt the cathedral and the town centre in [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] style.
lordship-of-faenza.e: In 1501 [[e:cesare-borgia|Cesare Borgia]] besieged Faenza, which surrendered; the young lord [[e:astorre-iii-manfredi|Astorre III Manfredi]] was taken to [[e:rome|Rome]] and murdered in 1502. [[e:venice|Venice]] held Faenza until 1509, when it passed to the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]].

lao-issara.t: The 'Free Laos' nationalist government formed in 1945 to resist the return of French rule, and the seedbed of Lao independence politics.
lao-issara.o: After the Japanese surrender, [[e:phetsarath-ratanavongsa|Prince Phetsarath]], [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Kingdom of Luang Phrabang]], declared the unification and independence of [[e:laos|Laos]]. When King [[e:sisavang-vong|Sisavang Vong]] sided with [[e:france|France]] and dismissed him, Phetsarath's supporters formed the Lao Issara government in [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Vientiane]] in October 1945 and deposed the king.
lao-issara.r: The provisional government, with [[e:khammao-vilay|Khammao Vilay]] as prime minister and princes [[e:souvanna-phouma|Souvanna Phouma]] and [[e:souphanouvong|Souphanouvong]] as ministers, had little money or army and relied on support from Vietnamese communities and the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]]. It adopted a constitution and briefly restored [[e:sisavang-vong|Sisavang Vong]] as constitutional monarch in April 1946.
lao-issara.e: French forces retook [[s:kingdom-of-vientiane|Vientiane]] and [[s:kingdom-of-luang-phrabang|Luang Prabang]] in April and May 1946, and the Lao Issara leaders fled to [[e:bangkok|Bangkok]], forming a government in exile. It dissolved in 1949, with [[e:souvanna-phouma|Souvanna Phouma]] returning to the [[s:kingdom-of-laos|Kingdom of Laos]] and [[e:souphanouvong|Souphanouvong]] founding the communist [[e:pathet-lao|Pathet Lao]].

la-venta.t: The leading Olmec centre after San Lorenzo, an island capital in the Tabasco swamps famous for its clay pyramid, colossal heads and buried jade offerings.
la-venta.o: La Venta rose on a small island in the [[e:tonala-river|Tonalá]] river marshes of [[e:tabasco|Tabasco]] from about 900 BCE, as [[s:san-lorenzo|San Lorenzo]] declined. Access to estuaries, fishing grounds and river routes supported a growing population and an elite that drew labour and goods from a wide area.
la-venta.r: Its ceremonial core, Complex A and the great clay pyramid, was laid out on a north-south axis. Rulers commissioned four colossal heads, altars showing figures emerging from caves, and stelae. Massive offerings of serpentine blocks, jade celts and mosaic pavements were buried beneath plazas, showing enormous investment in ritual. Jade and other prestige goods came from distant sources, including [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]].
la-venta.e: Around 400 BCE La Venta was abandoned and many monuments were damaged. The [[e:olmecs|Olmec]] heartland lost its leading role, but La Venta's art, ritual and ideas of kingship passed into [[e:epi-olmec-culture|Epi-Olmec]], Maya and other later traditions.

lanao-sultanates.t: Confederation of Maranao Muslim principalities around Lake Lanao in Mindanao that resisted Spanish and American conquest for three centuries.
lanao-sultanates.o: [[e:islam|Islam]] reached the [[e:maranao-people|Maranao people]] of the [[e:lake-lanao|Lake Lanao]] plateau from the [[s:maguindanao-sultanate|Maguindanao Sultanate]] and the Sulu coast in the 16th and 17th centuries. Local datus adopted the title of sultan and grouped their communities into the Pat a Pangampong ko Ranao, the four principalities of Bayabao, Masiu, Unayan and Baloi, which shared customary law and lineage ties.
lanao-sultanates.r: Authority was widely dispersed: dozens of sultans and datus ruled villages, balanced by councils, genealogy and Islamic law alongside [[e:adat|adat]]. No single ruler commanded the whole confederation. The [[e:maranao-people|Maranao]] were farmers, metalworkers and weavers, known for brass work, the okir carving style and the epic [[e:darangen|Darangen]].
lanao-sultanates.e: Spanish expeditions, notably that of 1639 and the campaign of 1891 to 1895, failed to subdue the lake. After 1898 the Americans fought the [[e:maranao-people|Maranao]] at [[e:battle-of-bayan|Bayang]] in 1902 and in later campaigns, bringing [[e:lanao|Lanao]] under the [[s:moro-province|Moro Province]] by 1904. Royal houses still survive with customary authority.

lanfang-republic.t: Self-governing Hakka mining polity in West Borneo, sometimes called the first republic in Asia, that lasted over a century.
lanfang-republic.o: [[e:luo-fangbo|Luo Fangbo]], a [[e:hakka-people|Hakka]] scholar and migrant from [[e:guangdong|Guangdong]], organised Chinese gold miners near [[s:pontianak-sultanate|Pontianak]] and in 1777 founded the Lanfang kongsi at Mandor. Allied with the Pontianak Sultanate, it grew into a substantial state controlling mines, farmland and trade routes inland.
lanfang-republic.r: Lanfang was headed by an elected leader (the taige) assisted by officials, and decisions involved consultation among its members, which has led some writers to call it a republic, though the label is debated. It levied taxes, administered justice and maintained a militia. Most of its people were [[e:hakka-people|Hakka]] miners and farmers, with temple worship to Chinese deities.
lanfang-republic.e: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] tolerated Lanfang as a semi-autonomous ally longer than other kongsis. When its leader [[e:liu-asheng|Liu Asheng]] died in 1884 they moved to take control, crushed resistance in 1884 to 1885 and annexed it into the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]].
